newsitem.title: FINLAND: Russia's security services declare war on crime.
newsitem.headline: Russia's security services declare war on crime.

text.p: Russia's domestic intelligence agency has declared open war on economic crime and corruption, and officials are even hinting a joint initiative with the United States could come out of this week's superpower summit.

Speaking ahead of a Helsinki summit between Russian President Boris Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton, Federal Intelligence Service (FSB) chief Nikolai Kovalyov said his agents planned a clampdown on the billion-dollar problem.
"We have declared an open war on crime and corruption," Kovalyov said at Wednesday's late-night briefing, a rare international appearance for the secretive security chief.
In comments to reporters after the news conference, Kovalyov said cooperation with the U.S. was growing and did not rule out a joint initiative emerging at the summit.
"It's absolutely obvious that no one can tackle crime alone," he said.
Economic crime and corruption, a police matter in most countries, have become a political issue in Russia and the government was set on fighting it, Kovalyov said.
But he said various aspects of the law to combat crimes in Russia were poor and needed to be backed up by politicians.
A U.S. study published on Wednesday said 40 percent of the Russian economy was controlled by organised criminals and billions of dollars were leaking out of the country's economy as a result.

Yeltsin has said mafia "godfathers" have hijacked the free market he created and has said he is determined to root out organised crime which is said to dominate legitimate and illegal economic sectors in Russia.

Kovalyov, appointed to his post at the domestic successor to the Soviet-era KGB in July 1996, said Russia had successfully fought crime through international cooperation with colleagues in Sweden and Finland.
"We issue a warning to organised criminals that we will not allow organised crime...every employee in the security service must strive for that."
Kovalyov's appearance signalled a new determination to wipe out the growing scourge of crime in Russia, which is viewed as a deterrent to more foreign investment.
The most damaging aspect of organised crime is its contribution to large-scale capital flight, which government sources have said could total as much as $150 million annually.
